issues.legal_issue: A transfer of a Mitakshara coparcener’s undivided interest to another coparcener, without the consent of the other coparceners, is valid when it is properly construed as a renunciation in favour of the remaining coparceners.
material_facts: The family was a Mitakshara coparcenary.
A coparcener transferred his entire undivided interest to his brother, another coparcener, while reserving a life interest for himself.
The transfer was intended for the benefit of the brother and his sons, who were the remaining coparceners.
The transfer was challenged as an invalid gift made without the other coparceners’ consent.
issues.conclusion: The transfer was valid because, on these facts, it was to be construed as a renunciation of the transferor’s undivided interest in favour of the brother and his sons; the consent of the other coparceners was immaterial. The appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Mitakshara law, a coparcener generally cannot gift an undivided interest in coparcenary property without the prior consent of the other coparceners; a gift made with such consent is valid. A coparcener may, however, renounce his interest in favour of the coparceners as a body, and a purported transfer to one coparcener may operate for the benefit of all the remaining coparceners. Mulla’s Hindu Law, 15th ed., Articles 258 and 264, was relied on. The Court also considered section 30 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, noting that it permits testamentary disposition but did not alter the restriction on gifts; section 6 was also discussed. The Court referred to Suraj Bunsi Koer v. Sheo Proshad Singh, Baba v. Timma, Ponnusami v. Thatha, and A. Perumalakkal v. Kumaresan Balakrishnan, and rejected the contrary proposition in G. Suryakantam v. G. Suryanarayanamurthy.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a gift of a coparcener’s entire undivided interest without consent, and the transfer is intended to benefit the recipient and the remaining coparceners, the transfer is valid as a renunciation.
